summary: Defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring remote bridging over PPP links. It is a standards-track proposal. It was replaced by RFC 2878.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules for two ends of a line to agree on joining two networks as if they were one. A newer version replaced it.

what ppp protocol number does bcp use
subtitle: How two ends of a PPP link agree to act as a remote bridge between LANs.

tldr.problem: Two LANs far apart can be joined by a point-to-point line, but PPP had no standard way for the two ends to agree to act as bridges and to carry whole LAN frames.
tldr.mechanism: The Bridging Control Protocol (BCP) is a PPP Network Control Protocol that negotiates bridging options, then carries each bridged LAN frame or spanning tree BPDU in its own PPP packet.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1638 was a Proposed Standard. It obsoleted RFC 1220 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 2878.

today: RFC 1638 is obsoleted by RFC 2878, so that is the RFC to read for the current definition. It was a Proposed Standard published in June 1994 and itself obsoleted RFC 1220. Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: Why PPP Needs a Bridging Protocol
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) carries multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links. It has an extensible Link Control Protocol (LCP) and a family of Network Control Protocols that set up and configure each network-layer protocol. RFC 1638 defines the one for remote bridging.

The RFC describes two bridging algorithms in common use: Transparent Bridging, standardized for extended LANs by IEEE 802.1, and Source Route Bridging, common on IEEE 802.5 Token Ring. IEEE 802.1D covers both, but neither IEEE standard defines how a remote bridge works. The IEEE 802.1G committee was addressing remote bridging, and the RFC notes that the proposal had not been approved as a standard.

For simplicity, the RFC discusses remote bridging as two remote bridges joined by a single line.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks join other networks together with a box called a bridge. This RFC says how two such boxes at the ends of a long wire should talk to each other.

sections.title: Methods of Bridging
sections.content:
A transparent bridge keeps a forwarding database of {address, interface} records built from the source address of each frame it sees. A frame whose destination is unknown is sent out of every interface except the one it arrived on. Redundant paths would cause trouble, so bridges run the Spanning Tree Protocol: one system is elected Root and emits Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs), and ports with a worse path to the Root are put in a hot standby state.

In source routing, the sending station puts the path into the frame in a Routing Information Field (RIF), and finds paths with Explorer frames. For a PPP line the RFC allows two models: the line as the link between two halves of a split bridge, or as a LAN segment between two independent bridges. Independent-bridge is the default. Using the split-bridge model requires successfully negotiating the Bridge-Identification option.

A device that translates between transparent bridging and source routing is treated as one or the other on the line, because IEEE 802 was not addressing such bridges.
sections.plainLanguage: One kind of bridge learns where everyone lives by watching the mail. Another kind puts the whole route on the envelope. The two ends of the wire have to know which kind they are.

sections.title: Traffic Services
sections.content:
The design includes several services for different kinds of systems.

  • LAN Frame Checksum preservation. The protocol is optimized so the final receiver sees the same LAN frame checksum (FCS) the original sender computed. Frames that have no FCS are tagged and carried across. A system that does not preserve the FCS strips the trailing four octets.
  • Tinygram compression. On low speed lines (64 KBPS and below), Ethernet or IEEE 802.3 frames below the minimum size are often padded with zero octets. The sender may remove the zeros and tag the frame, and the receiver puts zeros back before sending it onto a LAN. Compression is the sender's choice.
  • LAN identification. A 32-bit LAN ID labels a user community so that traffic is only emitted onto LANs of the same community. The RFC gives a domain value for each port, with a default of 1 and 0 and 0xffffffff reserved, and a checkDomain flag that filters output.

The RFC's example has two bridges joined by a WAN line, with LAN ID 1 for one pair of LANs and LAN ID 2 for another, so the two virtual LANs share the one line without mixing.
sections.plainLanguage: Some extras help the line: keep the error-check number intact, squeeze out boring padding, and keep different groups of users from seeing each other's traffic.

sections.title: How BCP Runs Over PPP
sections.content:
BCP works exactly like LCP except for a few changes. A BCP packet rides in the PPP Information field with PPP Protocol value hex 8031. Only Codes 1 through 7 are used (Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject). BCP packets cannot be exchanged until PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase, and early ones SHOULD be silently discarded.

Bridged traffic only flows once BCP is in the Opened state. It travels with PPP Protocol value hex 0031, one bridged LAN frame or BPDU per PPP packet.

  • MRU. There is no standard way to fragment bridged frames, so the link MUST negotiate an MRU large enough for the MAC types in use. Even Ethernet frames are bigger than the default PPP MRU of 1500 octets because they include MAC headers.
  • Ordering. Over multiple links, a sender that does not know whether a protocol needs ordering MUST act as if all do.
  • Monitoring. Magic Number Loopback Detection and Link-Quality-Monitoring are strongly recommended, because spanning tree BPDUs flow mostly one way.
  • Separate trees. A manager can stop BPDUs on a link to split two regions into separate spanning trees.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any bridge traffic goes through, both ends shake hands. Then each package is labeled so the other side knows it is a bridged LAN message.

sections.title: Bridged Frame and BPDU Formats
sections.content:
A bridged LAN frame starts, after the PPP header, with a flags and padding octet. The flags are F (LAN FCS present), I (LAN ID present) and Z (802.3 pad must be zero filled to minimum size), followed by a reserved bit that must be zero. The Pads field tells the receiver how many pad octets to strip, up to 15. Next comes a one-octet MAC Type, the optional 32-bit LAN ID, the destination and source MAC addresses, the LLC data and the optional LAN FCS. The 802.4, 802.5 and FDDI format adds a pad byte and a Frame Control octet.

The MAC Type values are listed in the figure below. For the higher numbered form of a type, an implementation MUST also support the lower numbered form, and a system MUST NOT send a MAC Type above 4 unless the peer announced it with MAC-Support.

A spanning tree BPDU is carried without MAC or LLC headers, behind a Spanning Tree Protocol field: 0201 for IEEE 802.1, 0203 for IBM Source Route Bridge and 0205 for DEC LANbridge 100. A system configured for no spanning tree protocol MUST silently discard all BPDUs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bridged package has a small label saying what kind of network it came from, whether it has an error-check number, and how much filler to throw away.

sections.title: BCP Configuration Options
sections.content:
BCP uses the same option format as LCP, with its own seven option types. If an option is missing from a Configure-Request, its default applies.

  • Bridge-Identification and Line-Identification carry a 12-bit LAN segment number and a 4-bit bridge number (Bridge-Identification) or a LAN segment number (Line-Identification). They MUST NOT be in the same Configure-Request. If the peers do not agree, BCP MUST NOT enter the Opened state.
  • MAC-Support advertises which MAC types a system will accept. It is advisory and MUST NOT be in a Configure-Nak.
  • Tinygram-Compression and LAN-Identification take a value of 1 (enabled) or 2 (disabled), and the two sides need not agree. By default compression is not allowed and LAN-Identification is disabled.
  • MAC-Address announces an address, or asks for one by sending 00-00-00-00-00-00.
  • Spanning-Tree-Protocol negotiates the version. When the two sides disagree, the lower numbered protocol is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends use a checklist of choices, such as which kinds of networks they accept and which spanning tree rules to follow, and they must agree on the key ones before starting.

items.label: Bridge-Identification
items.desc: Treats the two systems as halves of one source-route bridge.

items.label: Line-Identification
items.desc: Gives the line a LAN segment number.

items.label: MAC-Support
items.desc: Lists MAC types the sender will accept.

items.label: LAN-Identification
items.desc: Enable or disable the LAN ID field.

items.label: MAC-Address
items.desc: Announce or request a MAC address.

items.label: Spanning-Tree-Protocol
items.desc: Choose the spanning tree protocol version.
